metaDescription: Six handheld cordless leaf blowers compared on weight, airflow and battery: Milwaukee, DeWalt and value brands, from a 4 lb sweeper to a 650 CFM kit.
expertTake: The Milwaukee M18 Fuel 2724 is the handheld to buy if you want real power from a single pack, and the compact Milwaukee 0884 is the one to buy if weight is the problem. The LOSART 650 CFM kit is the value pick with two batteries at 4.4 lb, but its numbers are claims. Nothing in this class suits a lot with more than a half acre of trees.
introParagraphs: A handheld blower is the tool most households reach for first, because it needs no harness, starts instantly and fits on a shelf. The compromise is that every ounce of the machine, and the battery clipped to it, hangs from your wrist, so how it feels in the hand matters as much as how much air it moves.

The market splits into established tool brands that sell a bare tool, and value brands that bundle two batteries and a charger with big claims. Neither approach is wrong, but they answer different questions, and the right choice depends on whether you already own a battery platform.

products.name: Milwaukee M18 Fuel 2724 Handheld Blower 450 CFM 120 MPH
products.description:
The 2724 earns the top spot because it balances output and handling better than anything else here. It lists 450 CFM and 120 MPH from a brushless motor, with simple high and low speed settings, and it runs on the same M18 battery that powers Milwaukee's drills and saws. That makes it a sensible purchase for anyone who already owns packs.

In the hand, it is a conventional single-pack handheld, which keeps the weight in check. The maker says it clears debris from about 15 feet away, a useful reach for hedges and flower beds. Its figures are not the biggest on the page, but they are real and from a brand with a long track record.

Because the listing is for the bare tool, a battery and charger are extra. A 5.0Ah pack suits it well. Compared with the LOSART kit at a claimed 650 CFM, it will move less air on paper, but it comes with a proven service network and a parts supply that will still exist in five years. Brush the vents after use and keep the packs indoors in winter. A drop of cleaner on a cloth removes grass stains from the housing, which keeps the vents from clogging with sticky residue.
products.bestFor: Owners of M18 batteries who want a balanced, proven handheld.
pros: 450 CFM and 120 MPH from a brushless motor
Runs on the broad M18 battery family
cons: Less claimed airflow than value kits

products.name: Milwaukee M18 0884-20 Compact Blower 4 lb
products.description:
The 0884 is the handheld for people who care about weight first. Milwaukee lists it at about 4 pounds with dimensions of roughly 14 by 6 by 10 inches, which is small enough to store in a toolbox and light enough to use one-handed for a while. The listing gives no airflow figures, so I will not invent any.

Its purpose is clear from the shape: sweeping decks, driveways, garages and flower beds rather than clearing a lawn. Next to the 2724, it will move far less air, and next to a 650 CFM value kit it is plainly outclassed on paper. That is the tradeoff you accept for a tool that never tires your arm.

If you already own M18 packs, it is a cheap extra. Keep the nozzle clear and store the tool with the battery removed. It is the right choice for older users, small paved areas and anyone whose wrist limits how long they can hold a heavier tool, and it fits neatly into a drawer beside the batteries.
products.bestFor: Users who prioritise low weight over raw power.
pros: About 4 pounds, very easy on the wrist
cons: No airflow figures on the listing

products.name: LOSART Cordless Blower 650 CFM 1200W 4.4 lb 2x5.0Ah
products.description:
The LOSART kit puts an axial turbo fan in a 4.4 pound body and bundles two 20V 5.0Ah batteries with a fast charger. It lists 650 CFM and three speed levels, with a non-slip grip. On the face of it, that is more air than the Milwaukee, in a lighter package, with two batteries in the box.

The caution is the same as with any value brand: the figure is a manufacturer claim, and the brand has no track record. A 20V pack-based tool claiming 650 CFM should be read as a peak number. Treat the weight and the two-battery package as the real attractions, and the airflow as a bonus if it holds up.

For a small to mid-size lot, it may be all you need. Check the return policy, read the warranty, keep the intake clear and charge the packs after use, and do not leave the packs on the charger for days at a time. If it performs as listed, it is hard to beat for the money; if not, the return policy is your friend.
products.bestFor: Buyers wanting two batteries and a light body for the lowest outlay.
pros: Two 5.0Ah batteries and a fast charger
650 CFM claimed in a 4.4 pound body
cons: Packs do not fit other tool brands

products.name: DeWalt DCE100B 20V Max Compact Blower 100 CFM
products.description:
The DCE100B is the smallest handheld in the list and is designed more for workshops and jobsites than for leaves. It lists 100 CFM, a three-speed switch and a variable-speed trigger with a lock. DeWalt names tuck pointing and cleaning joints among its uses.

For a person with a garage or a bench, it is a useful pocket-sized cleaner. For a yard, it is underpowered. Compared with the 4 pound Milwaukee 0884, it is a similar idea, but the DeWalt gives a published airflow figure, and that figure is low.

If you already own 20V Max batteries, it is a cheap addition. Keep the nozzle clear and wear eye protection when moving grit. It is the right tool for dust and not for leaf piles. A mitre saw station, a window track and a vehicle interior are the kind of places where its small stream is an advantage rather than a limit.
products.bestFor: Workshops, garages and jobsite cleaning, not lawns.
cons: Only 100 CFM, no good for leaves

products.name: MTKOALA Cordless Blower 450 CFM 150 MPH 2x2.6Ah
products.description:
This MTKOALA kit claims 450 CFM and 150 MPH with two speed modes, an axial fan and turbo technology. It comes with two 2.6Ah batteries and a fast charger, which is a smaller capacity than the LOSART's 5.0Ah pair. The seller offers 36 months of free replacement rather than repair, an unusual and useful promise if it is honoured.

The claimed numbers match the Milwaukee 2724's 450 CFM, with 30 MPH more speed. If true, that would be a bargain, but small 2.6Ah batteries limit how long you can run at full output. Expect short sessions on the high setting, and plan to alternate packs every few minutes if you push it.

It is a reasonable choice for a patio or a small yard when you want two batteries and a replacement guarantee. Because the replacement offer is the seller's own, confirm how returns are shipped and who pays. Read the terms, keep proof of purchase and charge both packs before a job.
products.bestFor: Small yards where a replacement guarantee matters.
pros: Two batteries and a fast charger

buyingCriteria.explanation: A handheld blower is held out in front of you, so its weight, plus the battery, is what you feel. The Milwaukee 0884 weighs about 4 pounds and the LOSART 4.4 pounds, which is gentle. A heavier unit with a big battery can feel twice as heavy after ten minutes. Hold the tool at arm length for a minute before you decide. Pay attention to where the battery sits, because a pack mounted behind the grip balances differently from one under the handle, and a nose-heavy tool twists the wrist. If the listing has a photo of the underside, look at how the battery is mounted.

The Milwaukee and DeWalt listings are bare tools, while the LOSART, MTKOALA and similar kits include two batteries and a charger. Two packs mean you can swap and keep working, but small packs such as 2.6Ah run out fast. A bigger single pack often beats two small ones, so look at amp-hours, not just the count. As a rough rule, a single 5.0Ah pack outlasts two 2.0Ah packs on most blowers, and a heavy user will want a spare anyway. Buying a bigger pack later is easy on a platform, but not on a closed value kit.

The Milwaukee 2724 lists 450 CFM from a brushless 18V design. The LOSART claims 650 CFM from a 20V pack, which is a very high figure for that class. Value brands often quote turbo peaks. Treat any number from a brand you cannot verify as an upper bound, and plan around a middle value. One sensible check is to ask how a 20V pack can feed a motor that claims 1200W, since the arithmetic only works for a short burst. That does not make the tool bad, but it does tell you the top figure is not a working speed.

The Milwaukee has high and low, the LOSART three levels, the MTKOALA two modes and the DeWalt a three-speed switch with a variable trigger. A lower setting is gentler near plants and saves battery. If you work around flower beds and furniture, a variable trigger or three steps is better than two. A blower on high will strip mulch from a bed in seconds, so being able to drop to a gentle stream saves cleanup afterwards.

A brand platform like M18 or 20V Max gives you access to dozens of other tools using the same pack. A value brand's battery usually fits only its own tools. If you plan to add a trimmer or a drill, buy into a platform. The cost of the tools you add later is lower when the pack is already in your hand, and that saving usually outweighs a small difference in blower price. If the blower is a one-off, a bundled kit is fine.

An established brand offers service centres and a multi-year warranty. A value brand may offer a replacement promise, such as the 36 months from MTKOALA, but only the seller stands behind it. Read how a claim works, and keep the packaging for a while after buying. Take a photo of the serial plate on day one, since some sellers ask for it when you ask for a replacement.

specDecoder.meaning: Cubic feet per minute, the volume of air at the nozzle. It indicates how much material the blower can move.
specDecoder.watchFor: A value-brand figure may be a peak, so do not compare it directly with a branded tool's.

specDecoder.meaning: The speed of air leaving the nozzle. It lifts stuck debris.
specDecoder.watchFor: Speed drops off quickly with distance from the nozzle.

specDecoder.meaning: Battery capacity. A 5.0Ah pack holds about twice as much energy as a 2.6Ah pack at the same voltage.
specDecoder.watchFor: Two 2.6Ah batteries hold less total energy than two 5.0Ah.

specDecoder.meaning: A motor power figure used by some brands. It does not directly tell you airflow.
specDecoder.watchFor: Do not compare watts across brands.

specDecoder.meaning: A listing for the tool alone, without battery or charger.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Milwaukee and DeWalt here are bare, so add the cost of a pack.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated weights, from about 4 pounds on the Milwaukee 0884 to 4.4 pounds on the LOSART. Fatigue is the main reason people stop using a handheld, so this carried real weight.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at CFM and MPH and noted which came from a known brand. The 2724's 450 CFM and 120 MPH are firm figures, and value-kit claims were treated as claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery package
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared what each kit includes. Two batteries and a charger change the real cost, and amp-hours matter more than count.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform value
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how each battery fits other tools. M18 and 20V Max earned credit for breadth, and value brands lost some for isolation.

howWeEvaluated.title: Support and honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed warranty and brand history. Where a listing gave no figure, we said so.

cards.label: Brand platform
cards.text: The Milwaukee and DeWalt tools use batteries that run many other tools. You pay for the platform and get durability and support.

cards.label: Bundled kit
cards.text: The LOSART and MTKOALA put two batteries in the box for less. The packs work only with their own tools and the brand has no long history.

howToChoose.note: Pick a platform if you will add tools; pick a kit for a one-off, light-duty blower.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Low weight with the battery on, a non-slip grip and a balanced body. A tool you can hold for 20 minutes is better than a stronger one you drop after five.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Milwaukee 0884 at about 4 pounds and the LOSART at 4.4 pounds are the lightest. The 2724 is heavier but still manageable.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You will add tools to the same battery platform or want long-term support. The Milwaukee 2724 is the pick.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You need a light-duty blower for a small yard. The LOSART or MTKOALA kit covers it.

maintenance.why: Debris blocks the intake and heats the motor. A quick wipe restores airflow, and it takes five seconds with a dry brush.
Using packs in turn avoids deep discharge. Two-battery kits make this easy.
Lithium packs age fastest when full or empty. Keep them indoors above freezing.
Sweat and dust make the grip slippery. A damp cloth keeps it secure, which matters when the tool is held out at arm length for a long job.
Value-brand replacement offers require proof of purchase. A folder in the garage is enough.

faq.q: What is the best handheld leaf blower overall?
faq.a: The Milwaukee M18 Fuel 2724 is the best balanced, with 450 CFM and 120 MPH and an established brand behind it. For the lightest option, the 0884 at about 4 pounds is better.

Some are fine for light use, but their claims are unverified and support can be thin. A good sign is a seller that publishes the battery capacity, the charger rating and the weight, and a poor sign is a listing with only a big airflow number. Read the return policy and warranty before you commit.

faq.q: How long does a handheld blower run?
faq.a: It depends on battery size and speed. Small 2.0 to 2.6Ah packs last minutes at full output, and larger 5.0Ah packs last far longer.
For a small yard, one is enough, provided the pack is a decent size. For anything over 15 minutes, a second pack helps, or a single larger pack.

faq.q: Can I use a handheld blower on wet leaves?
faq.a: Only lightly. Wet leaves are heavy and sticky. High air speed matters most, and handhelds in this guide are better for dry leaves.

faq.q: Is the DeWalt DCE100B a leaf blower?
faq.a: It is a compact blower for dust and small areas, with 100 CFM. For leaves, choose a stronger model.
